I Replaced My Entire Development Workflow With Cursor — Here's What Actually Happened

Cursor promises to replace traditional coding. After one month using it for my web projects, here's the brutal truth about what works and what doesn't.

The Promise

Every developer I know is talking about Cursor. It's being called "the end of coding as we know it." As someone who also directs films and manages a production company, I was skeptical. I've seen too many tools promise to replace creative work.

But I've been using Cursor for my web development work for the past month. Here's what actually happened.

What Works

Speed of iteration: I can describe what I want in plain English and get working code. Not pseudocode. Not "almost working" code. Working code that I can actually use.

Learning tool: I'm not a programmer by training. I've learned more about how web development actually works in one month with Cursor than in years of trying to teach myself. It explains what it's doing while it does it.

Refactoring: I have old code from 2019 that I was afraid to touch. Cursor refactored an entire component library in an afternoon. It would have taken me a week.

What Doesn't Work

Complex architecture: For big picture planning, you still need a human. Cursor is brilliant at executing a vision. Terrible at creating one.

Debugging errors it created: Here's the irony: when Cursor creates bugs, they're often harder to fix than bugs I'd create myself. Because the logic is complex and the AI doesn't always explain its reasoning.

Security concerns: You're feeding your codebase to an AI. I use Cursor for open-source projects only. For client work with NDAs, I'm more careful.

The Verdict

Cursor isn't replacing developers. It's replacing the parts of development that developers hate: boilerplate, repetitive patterns, documentation, basic CRUD operations.

What it can't replace: creative problem-solving, architectural decisions, understanding client needs, and the judgment to know when code is right.

For me? It's now my primary tool. But I'm clear-eyed about what it is: an incredibly powerful assistant, not a replacement.

Rating: 8/10 — Essential for modern development. Just know its limits.
